structures.name: right atrium
structures.definition: Upper right chamber of the heart, receiving blood from the venae cavae and the coronary sinus.
structures.function: Collects deoxygenated blood from the body and pushes it into the right ventricle.
structures.why: A thin-walled reservoir lets blood keep flowing into the heart while the ventricles are contracting.

notes.medicine: Contains the sinoatrial node, the heart’s natural pacemaker, near the opening of the superior vena cava.
notes.nursing: Central venous pressure reflects the pressure in this chamber; central line tips sit just above it.

structures.name: left atrium
structures.definition: Upper left chamber of the heart, at the back, receiving the four pulmonary veins.
structures.function: Collects oxygenated blood from the lungs and pushes it into the left ventricle.
structures.why: It acts as a booster pump, topping up the left ventricle just before it contracts.

notes.medicine: In atrial fibrillation clots form in its appendage, the source of most cardioembolic strokes.
notes.sports: Endurance training enlarges it modestly as part of the “athlete’s heart”.

structures.name: right ventricle
structures.definition: Lower right chamber of the heart, forming most of its front surface.
structures.function: Pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary valve to the lungs.
structures.why: The lungs need only low pressure, so its wall is thin and it pumps at about a fifth of the left side’s pressure.

notes.medicine: Fails when lung pressure rises (cor pulmonale), causing raised neck veins, liver congestion and ankle swelling.
notes.nursing: Right-sided heart failure shows as peripheral oedema and a raised jugular venous pressure.

structures.name: left ventricle
structures.definition: Lower left chamber of the heart, forming its apex, with the thickest muscular wall.
structures.function: Pumps oxygenated blood through the aortic valve to the whole body.
structures.why: Its thick wall generates the high pressure needed to push blood to every organ.

notes.medicine: Left ventricular failure backs fluid into the lungs, causing breathlessness and pulmonary oedema.
notes.nursing: Orthopnoea and crackles at the lung bases suggest left-sided heart failure.
notes.sports: Endurance training enlarges its cavity; strength training thickens its wall.

structures.name: tricuspid valve
structures.definition: Three-leaflet valve between the right atrium and right ventricle.
structures.function: Lets blood pass into the right ventricle and closes to stop it flowing back when the ventricle contracts.
structures.why: Its closure, with the mitral valve’s, makes the first heart sound.

notes.medicine: Infective endocarditis of this valve is typical of people who inject drugs.

structures.name: mitral valve
structures.definition: Two-leaflet valve between the left atrium and left ventricle.
structures.function: Lets oxygenated blood into the left ventricle and seals as the ventricle contracts.
structures.why: It withstands the highest pressure of any valve, held shut by cords anchored to papillary muscles.

notes.medicine: Mitral regurgitation gives a pansystolic murmur heard best at the apex, radiating to the axilla.

structures.name: pulmonary valve
structures.definition: Three-cusp valve at the exit of the right ventricle.
structures.function: Opens to let blood into the pulmonary trunk and closes to stop it falling back.
structures.why: Its pocket-shaped cusps fill with blood and snap shut without needing cords.

notes.medicine: Its closure contributes to the second heart sound, best heard at the left upper sternal edge.

structures.name: aortic valve
structures.definition: Three-cusp valve at the exit of the left ventricle.
structures.function: Opens to let blood into the aorta and closes to stop it falling back into the ventricle.
structures.why: The coronary arteries arise just above its cusps, so the heart feeds itself when the valve closes.

notes.medicine: Aortic stenosis causes an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, with angina, syncope and breathlessness.

structures.name: papillary muscles
structures.definition: Finger-like muscles projecting from the ventricular walls, attached by cords to the valve leaflets.
structures.function: Tense the cords as the ventricles contract so the leaflets don’t flip back into the atria.
structures.why: Without them the inlet valves would blow inside out under ventricular pressure.

notes.medicine: Rupture after a myocardial infarction causes sudden severe mitral regurgitation.

structures.name: ascending aorta
structures.definition: First part of the aorta, rising from the left ventricle behind the sternum.
structures.function: Carries all the blood leaving the left ventricle and gives off the coronary arteries.
structures.why: Its elastic wall stretches with each beat and recoils to keep blood moving between beats.

notes.medicine: Dilates in Marfan syndrome and with age; dissection here is a surgical emergency.

structures.name: aortic arch
structures.definition: Curved part of the aorta that turns backwards and to the left over the root of the left lung.
structures.function: Gives off the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries to the head and arms.
structures.why: Curving over lets one vessel supply the head and arms and then descend to the body.

notes.medicine: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under it, so an aneurysm here can cause hoarseness.

structures.name: descending aorta
structures.definition: Part of the aorta running down through the back of the chest beside the vertebral column.
structures.function: Carries blood to the chest wall, oesophagus and then on to the abdomen.
structures.why: Running along the spine keeps it protected and lets it supply the body segment by segment.

notes.medicine: Becomes the abdominal aorta as it passes through the diaphragm at T12.

structures.name: pulmonary trunk
structures.definition: Large artery leaving the right ventricle that divides into right and left branches.
structures.function: Carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
structures.why: It is the only artery that carries deoxygenated blood (apart from the umbilical arteries before birth).

notes.medicine: A large clot lodged where it divides (saddle embolus) causes sudden collapse.

structures.name: pulmonary veins
structures.definition: Four veins, two from each lung, opening into the back of the left atrium.
structures.function: Return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart.
structures.why: They are the only veins carrying oxygen-rich blood.

notes.medicine: Catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation isolates the openings of these veins.

structures.name: superior vena cava
structures.definition: Large vein entering the top of the right atrium.
structures.function: Returns blood from the head, neck, arms and upper chest.
structures.why: One short, wide vein lets blood from the whole upper body drain into the heart with little resistance.

notes.nursing: The tip of a central venous catheter should lie in its lower part, just above the right atrium.
notes.medicine: Obstruction (often by lung cancer) causes face and arm swelling and distended chest veins.

structures.name: inferior vena cava
structures.definition: The largest vein, entering the bottom of the right atrium after passing through the diaphragm.
structures.function: Returns blood from the legs, pelvis and abdomen.
structures.why: It carries the largest volume of returning blood, so it is the widest vein in the body.

notes.nursing: In late pregnancy, lying flat compresses it; tilt the patient to the left.
notes.medicine: Ultrasound of its diameter and collapse helps assess fluid status.

structures.name: brachiocephalic trunk
structures.definition: First and largest branch of the aortic arch, on the right side.
structures.function: Divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.
structures.why: Gives the right side of the head and the right arm one shared origin from the aorta.

notes.medicine: There is only one: the left carotid and subclavian arteries arise directly from the arch.

structures.name: right coronary artery
structures.definition: Artery arising above the aortic valve and running in the groove between the right atrium and ventricle.
structures.function: Supplies the right atrium, right ventricle and, in most people, the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes.
structures.why: Running in the groove around the heart protects it while it supplies the right side.

notes.medicine: Its blockage causes inferior myocardial infarction (ST elevation in II, III, aVF) and often heart block.

structures.name: left coronary artery
structures.definition: Short main artery arising above the aortic valve and passing behind the pulmonary trunk.
structures.function: Divides into the anterior interventricular and circumflex branches that feed the left heart.
structures.why: Supplies the hard-working left ventricle, which needs the most oxygen.

notes.medicine: A blockage of the left main stem threatens a large area of muscle and is often treated surgically.

structures.name: left anterior descending artery
structures.definition: Branch running down the groove on the front of the heart between the two ventricles.
structures.function: Supplies the front of the left ventricle, the apex and the front two-thirds of the septum.
structures.why: It feeds the largest share of the left ventricle’s muscle.

notes.medicine: Called the “widow-maker”: its blockage causes large anterior infarctions (ST elevation V1–V4).

structures.name: circumflex artery
structures.definition: Branch of the left coronary artery that curves around the left side of the heart in the groove between atrium and ventricle.
structures.function: Supplies the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle.
structures.why: Wrapping around the heart lets one vessel reach its left and back walls.

notes.medicine: Its blockage causes lateral infarction and can be electrically silent on a standard ECG.

structures.name: posterior descending artery
structures.definition: Artery running in the groove on the underside of the heart between the ventricles.
structures.function: Supplies the back third of the septum and the inferior wall of both ventricles.
structures.why: Whichever coronary artery gives this branch is called “dominant” — usually the right.

notes.medicine: Coronary dominance is defined by which artery gives rise to it.

structures.name: coronary sinus
structures.definition: Wide venous channel in the groove on the back of the heart, opening into the right atrium.
structures.function: Collects most of the blood that has supplied the heart muscle and returns it to the right atrium.
structures.why: The heart drains its own veins straight back into itself.

notes.medicine: Pacing leads for cardiac resynchronisation therapy are passed through it to reach the left ventricle.
